531	**3.5 Waste Management**
532	
533	Terraverde generates both hazardous and non-hazardous waste in the course of our manufacturing operations. We are committed to minimizing waste generation at the source, maximizing the recycling and recovery of waste materials, and ensuring that all waste streams are managed in full compliance with applicable federal and state regulations, including the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) and state counterpart regulations.
534	
535	**Hazardous Waste**
536	
537	In fiscal year 2024, Terraverde generated a total of 14,820 metric tons of hazardous waste across our six manufacturing facilities. Of this total, 3,410 metric tons, or 23.0%, were recycled or reclaimed through licensed hazardous waste recycling facilities. Hazardous waste streams generated by our operations include spent solvents, off-specification chemical products, process residues, contaminated materials, and lab waste.
538	
539	All hazardous waste is characterized, labeled, stored, and disposed of in strict compliance with RCRA regulations and applicable state hazardous waste rules. Our facilities maintain hazardous waste storage areas that meet RCRA standards for containment, labeling, and inspection. We use only licensed and insured transporters and treatment, storage, and disposal facilities (TSDFs) for all hazardous waste shipments, and we maintain detailed waste manifests and shipping records as required by regulation.
540	
541	**Non-Hazardous Waste**
542	
543	Terraverde generated 41,670 metric tons of non-hazardous waste in FY2024. Of this total, 22,090 metric tons, or 53.0%, were diverted from landfill through recycling, composting, or beneficial reuse. Non-hazardous waste streams include packaging materials (cardboard, plastic, pallets), office waste, maintenance waste, construction debris, and non-hazardous process residues.
544	
545	Our waste diversion efforts are supported by facility-level recycling programs, partnerships with waste recyclers and material recovery facilities, and employee engagement programs that promote waste segregation and recycling at the source.
546	
547	  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
548	  **Waste Category**              **FY2024 (Metric Tons)**   **Recycled / Diverted**   **Rate**
549	  ------------------------------- -------------------------- ------------------------- -----------------
550	  Hazardous Waste Generated       14,820                     3,410                     23.0%
551	
552	  Non-Hazardous Waste Generated   41,670                     22,090                    53.0%
553	  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
554	
555	**Waste Minimization**
556	
557	Terraverde is committed to reducing waste generation at the source through process optimization, raw material efficiency improvements, and product reformulation where feasible. We have established waste minimization teams at each manufacturing facility tasked with identifying opportunities to reduce waste generation, increase material efficiency, and improve recycling rates. We are also working with our supply chain partners to reduce packaging waste and explore opportunities for closed-loop material recovery programs.
558	
559	We will continue to report on our waste generation and recycling performance annually and will evaluate establishing formal waste reduction targets in future reporting periods.
560	
561	**[Section 4]{.underline}**
562	
563	**[Social Responsibility]{.underline}**
564	
565	At Terraverde, our people are the foundation of our success. We are committed to fostering a workplace that is safe, inclusive, and empowering --- one that attracts top talent, supports professional development, and enables our employees to contribute their best work every day. Our social responsibility commitments extend beyond our workforce to the communities in which we operate, where we strive to be a positive and engaged corporate neighbor.
566	
567	This section of our ESG report provides an overview of our workforce composition, diversity and inclusion efforts, health and safety performance, and community engagement programs.
568	
569	\[Infographic placeholder: Collage of employee photos from manufacturing facilities and corporate offices\]
570	
571	**4.1 Our Workforce**
572	
573	As of December 31, 2024, Terraverde employed approximately 3,100 people across our seven locations. Our employees are the driving force behind our company\'s success, and we are committed to attracting, developing, and retaining a talented and diverse workforce that shares our values and our commitment to operational excellence.
574	
575	Our workforce is distributed across our facilities as follows:
576	
577	  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
578	  **Facility**                       **Location**            **Employees**
579	  ---------------------------------- ----------------------- -----------------------
580	  Corporate Headquarters & R&D Lab   Charlotte, NC           320
581	
582	  Plant 1 --- Gastonia               Gastonia, NC            485
583	
584	  Plant 2 --- Greenville             Greenville, SC          612
585	
586	  Plant 3 --- Savannah               Savannah, GA            378
587	
588	  Plant 4 --- Huntsville             Huntsville, AL          541
589	
590	  Plant 5 --- Tuscaloosa             Tuscaloosa, AL          267
591	
592	  Plant 6 --- Chattanooga            Chattanooga, TN         398
593	  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
594	
595	Approximately 87% of our employees are based at our six manufacturing facilities, with the remaining 13% at our Charlotte headquarters and R&D lab. Our manufacturing workforce includes production operators, process engineers, maintenance technicians, quality assurance specialists, and EHS professionals, among other roles. Our corporate workforce includes employees in finance, legal, human resources, information technology, marketing, sales, supply chain, and sustainability functions.
596	
597	**Workforce Diversity**
598	
599	We are proud of the diversity of our workforce. As of December 31, 2024:
600	
601	> • **34% of our total workforce is female**, reflecting our ongoing efforts to recruit, develop, and advance women across all functional areas and levels of our organization.
602	>
603	> • **29% of our total workforce identifies as racially or ethnically diverse**, including employees who identify as Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, Asian, Native American, or two or more races.
604	
605	We recognize that a diverse workforce drives innovation, strengthens decision-making, and enhances our ability to serve our customers and communities. We are committed to building on the diversity of our current workforce and to continuing to advance our diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, as described further in Section 4.2.
606	
607	**Talent Development and Training**
608	
609	Terraverde invests in the professional growth and development of our employees through a comprehensive suite of training and development programs. Our training programs include:
610	
611	> • **New employee orientation and onboarding**: All new hires complete a multi-day orientation program that covers company values, safety protocols, regulatory compliance, and job-specific technical training.
612	>
613	> • **Technical skills training**: Manufacturing employees receive ongoing technical training on equipment operation, process safety, quality control, and maintenance procedures.
614	>
615	> • **Leadership development**: We offer leadership development programs for mid-level and senior managers, including mentoring, executive coaching, and participation in external leadership forums.
616	>
617	> • **Tuition reimbursement**: Terraverde provides tuition reimbursement for employees pursuing undergraduate and graduate degrees in fields relevant to their roles.
618	
619	**Employee Engagement**
620	
621	We conduct an annual employee engagement survey to measure employee satisfaction, identify areas for improvement, and track progress on key engagement metrics over time. In our most recent survey, conducted in October 2024, we achieved a participation rate of 82% and an overall engagement score that exceeded industry benchmarks for specialty chemicals manufacturers.
622	
623	We are committed to maintaining an open and transparent dialogue with our employees and to acting on the feedback we receive through our engagement surveys and other listening channels.
624	
625	**4.2 Diversity and Inclusion**
626	
627	Terraverde is committed to building a diverse, equitable, and inclusive workplace where every employee feels valued, respected, and empowered to contribute to their fullest potential. We believe that diversity of thought, experience, and background strengthens our organization and drives better outcomes for our business, our customers, and our communities.
628	
629	**Board of Directors**
630	
631	Our Board of Directors reflects our commitment to diversity at the highest levels of our organization. As of December 31, 2024, our nine-member Board includes:
632	
633	> • **3 female directors** (33.3% of the Board)
634	>
635	> • **2 directors who identify as racially or ethnically diverse** (22.2% of the Board)
636	
637	Our Board is committed to ensuring that its composition reflects a broad range of perspectives, skills, and backgrounds. The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee considers diversity as a factor in evaluating potential director candidates, including diversity of gender, race, ethnicity, age, professional experience, and geographic background.
638	
639	**Senior Leadership**
640	
641	Our senior leadership team (Vice President level and above) consists of 28 individuals, of whom:
642	
643	> • **9 are female** (32.1%)
644	>
645	> • **7 identify as racially or ethnically diverse** (25.0%)
646	
647	We are focused on building a robust pipeline of diverse talent for senior leadership positions through targeted recruitment, sponsorship and mentoring programs, and developmental assignments that prepare high-potential employees for advancement.
648	
649	**Total Workforce**
650	
651	As noted in Section 4.1, our total workforce is 34% female and 29% racially or ethnically diverse. We are committed to continuing to improve representation at all levels of our organization, with particular focus on increasing diversity in technical, engineering, and manufacturing leadership roles.
652	
653	**DEI Initiatives**
654	
655	Terraverde has implemented a range of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, including:
656	
657	> • **Employee Resource Groups (ERGs)**: We support four active ERGs --- Women at Terraverde, the Black Employee Network, the Hispanic/Latino Alliance, and the Veterans Network. These ERGs provide community, professional development opportunities, and a platform for advocacy and awareness.
658	>
659	> • **Inclusive Recruitment**: We have expanded our recruiting partnerships to include Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), and professional organizations focused on underrepresented groups in STEM fields.
660	>
661	> • **Unconscious Bias Training**: All managers and supervisors participate in annual unconscious bias training to promote equitable decision-making in hiring, performance evaluation, and talent development.
662	>
663	> • **Pay Equity Reviews**: We conduct annual pay equity reviews to identify and address any unjustified disparities in compensation based on gender, race, or ethnicity.
664	
665	We are committed to transparency regarding our diversity metrics and will continue to report on our workforce composition, leadership diversity, and DEI program progress in future ESG reports.
666	
667	**4.3 Health and Safety**
668	
669	The health and safety of our employees is Terraverde\'s highest priority. We operate in an industry where workplace hazards --- including chemical exposure, thermal burns, falls, and machinery-related injuries --- are inherent, and we are committed to providing a safe working environment through rigorous safety management, comprehensive training, and a culture of personal accountability.
670	
671	**Safety Performance**
672	
673	Terraverde\'s safety performance for fiscal year 2024 is summarized in the following table:
674	
675	  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
676	  **Safety Metric**                                   **FY2024**
677	  --------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
678	  Total Recordable Incident Rate (TRIR)               1.82
679	
680	  Days Away, Restricted, or Transferred (DART) Rate   0.91
681	
682	  Total Recordable Incidents                          52
683	
684	  Total Hours Worked                                  5,762,000
685	
686	  Fatalities                                          0
687	  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
688	
689	Our TRIR of 1.82 reflects our continued focus on workplace safety and represents improvement over industry averages. The TRIR is calculated as the number of OSHA-recordable incidents per 200,000 hours worked, consistent with the methodology prescribed by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). We are pleased to report zero fatalities among our employees and contractors in FY2024.
690	
691	Our DART rate of 0.91 --- measuring incidents that result in days away from work, restricted duty, or transfer to another job --- indicates that approximately half of our recordable incidents resulted in some degree of lost time or work restriction. We continue to focus on reducing both the frequency and severity of workplace incidents.
692	
693	**Safety Culture and Management**
694	
695	Our approach to workplace safety is grounded in a strong safety culture that emphasizes personal responsibility, hazard recognition, and proactive risk management. Key elements of our safety program include:
696	
697	> • **Safety Leadership**: Facility general managers are accountable for safety performance at their sites, with safety metrics incorporated into management performance evaluations and compensation decisions.
698	>
699	> • **Behavioral Safety Observations**: We have implemented a behavioral-based safety observation program at all manufacturing facilities, in which employees and supervisors conduct regular observations of work practices and provide real-time coaching and feedback.
700	>
701	> • **Job Safety Analysis (JSA)**: High-risk tasks and non-routine work activities require completion of a job safety analysis prior to commencement, ensuring that hazards are identified and appropriate controls are in place.
702	>
703	> • **Incident Investigation**: All recordable incidents and significant near-miss events are investigated using a structured root cause analysis methodology. Corrective and preventive actions are tracked to completion and shared across facilities to promote organizational learning.
704	>
705	> • **Safety Training**: All manufacturing employees receive annual safety training covering topics including hazard communication, personal protective equipment, lockout/tagout, confined space entry, fall protection, and emergency response. New employees complete comprehensive safety orientation before being authorized to work in production areas.
706	
707	We are committed to continuous improvement in our safety performance and have set a long-term goal of zero recordable incidents across all of our operations. While we recognize that achieving this goal will require sustained focus and investment, we believe it is the only acceptable aspiration for a company that places the safety and well-being of its people at the center of its values.
708	
709	**4.4 Community Engagement**
710	
711	Terraverde is committed to being a responsible and engaged corporate citizen in the communities where we live and work. Our six manufacturing facilities are located in communities across the southeastern United States, and we recognize that our success is intertwined with the vitality and well-being of these communities. We strive to contribute positively through philanthropic giving, volunteerism, educational partnerships, and environmental stewardship activities.
712	
713	**STEM Education Partnerships**
714	
715	We believe that investing in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education is essential to building the skilled workforce of the future and to strengthening the communities around our facilities. Terraverde partners with local school districts, community colleges, and universities near our manufacturing sites to support STEM education through:
716	
717	> • Sponsorship of science fairs, robotics competitions, and engineering design challenges at local high schools
718	>
719	> • Hosting facility tours and career day events for students and educators
720	>
721	> • Providing summer internship opportunities for college students pursuing degrees in chemistry, chemical engineering, environmental science, and related fields
722	>
723	> • Contributing to scholarship funds at community colleges and technical schools in our facility communities
724	
725	**Environmental Stewardship Volunteering**
726	
727	Terraverde employees are active participants in environmental stewardship and community beautification projects in their local communities. In FY2024, employee volunteer teams participated in stream cleanups, tree planting events, park restoration projects, and habitat conservation activities across our facility communities. We encourage employee volunteerism through our paid volunteer time-off program, which provides each employee up to 16 hours of paid time annually for community service activities.
728	
729	**Charitable Giving**
730	
731	Terraverde\'s corporate giving program supports nonprofit organizations in our facility communities with a focus on education, environmental conservation, health and human services, and community development. In FY2024, Terraverde and the Terraverde Foundation collectively contributed approximately \$1.2 million in charitable grants and sponsorships to organizations across our seven-state operating region.
732	
733	We are proud of the role our company and our employees play in strengthening the communities we call home, and we are committed to expanding our community engagement programs in the years ahead.
734	
735	**[Section 5]{.underline}**
736	
737	**[Governance]{.underline}**
738	
739	**5.1 Board Oversight of ESG**
740	
741	Strong corporate governance is the foundation upon which Terraverde\'s business strategy, risk management, and stakeholder accountability are built. Our Board of Directors is actively engaged in overseeing the company\'s ESG strategy and ensuring that sustainability considerations are integrated into our long-term business planning and risk management processes.

743	**Board Composition and Structure**
744	
745	Terraverde\'s Board of Directors consists of nine members, a majority of whom are independent directors. The Board operates through four standing committees: the Audit Committee, the Compensation Committee, the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, and the Technology and Innovation Committee. Each committee is composed entirely of independent directors and operates under a written charter that defines its responsibilities and authority.
746	
747	**ESG Oversight**
748	
749	The Board has assigned primary oversight responsibility for ESG matters, including sustainability reporting and climate-related risk management, to the Audit Committee. The Audit Committee chair has been a leading advocate for enhanced ESG disclosure and played a pivotal role in the decision to produce this inaugural standalone ESG report. The Audit Committee receives quarterly updates from Marcus Okonkwo, VP Sustainability & EHS, on the status of the company\'s sustainability initiatives, environmental compliance, GHG emissions performance, and ESG reporting activities.
750	
751	The full Board of Directors reviews and discusses the company\'s overall ESG strategy and key sustainability metrics at least annually, typically in connection with the Board\'s annual strategic planning session. In FY2024, the Board took several significant actions related to ESG, including:
752	
753	> • **September 12, 2024**: The Board approved Terraverde\'s greenhouse gas reduction targets, including the 30% reduction in combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 2030 and the net-zero by 2050 aspiration (see Section 3.2.4).
754	>
755	> • **December 2024**: The Board reviewed and approved the scope and timeline for the company\'s inaugural ESG report and authorized its planned publication and SEC filing.
756	
757	The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee oversees the company\'s governance framework, including Board composition, director independence, and director diversity considerations. The Compensation Committee considers ESG performance factors in the design of executive compensation programs, including safety performance metrics and environmental compliance.
758	
759	**Risk Management**
760	
761	Terraverde\'s enterprise risk management (ERM) framework identifies, assesses, and monitors a range of strategic, operational, financial, and compliance risks, including risks related to climate change, environmental regulation, and sustainability. Our ERM process is overseen by the Audit Committee, which receives periodic risk assessments from management and evaluates the adequacy of the company\'s risk mitigation strategies.
762	
763	Climate-related risks are assessed as part of our broader ERM process and include both physical risks (e.g., extreme weather events, water stress) and transition risks (e.g., regulatory changes, carbon pricing, shifting customer preferences). We are committed to further integrating climate risk assessment into our strategic planning processes and will provide expanded climate risk disclosures in future reporting periods.
764	
765	**Management Accountability**
766	
767	Day-to-day management of Terraverde\'s sustainability program is led by Marcus Okonkwo, VP Sustainability & EHS, who reports directly to our Chief Operating Officer and has a dotted-line reporting relationship to the Audit Committee. Marcus leads a cross-functional sustainability team that includes representatives from environmental health & safety, operations, finance, legal, and investor relations. This team is responsible for setting sustainability priorities, managing data collection and reporting, driving emissions reduction initiatives, and engaging with stakeholders on ESG matters.
768	
769	Our CEO and senior leadership team are committed to advancing Terraverde\'s sustainability agenda and view ESG performance as integral to the company\'s long-term value creation strategy.
770	
771	**5.2 Ethics and Compliance**
772	
773	Terraverde is committed to conducting its business with the highest standards of integrity, ethics, and compliance with applicable laws and regulations. We believe that ethical conduct and a strong culture of compliance are essential to maintaining the trust of our stakeholders and to sustaining our long-term business success.
774	
775	**Code of Conduct**
776	
777	Terraverde\'s Code of Conduct establishes the ethical standards and behavioral expectations that apply to all employees, officers, and directors of the company. The Code covers a wide range of topics, including conflicts of interest, fair dealing, protection of company assets, confidentiality, insider trading, anti-bribery and anti-corruption, environmental compliance, workplace safety, and respect in the workplace. All employees are required to complete annual Code of Conduct training and to certify their compliance with the Code.
778	
779	**Anti-Corruption**
780	
781	Terraverde maintains a comprehensive anti-corruption compliance program designed to ensure compliance with the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the U.K. Bribery Act, and other applicable anti-corruption laws. Our anti-corruption program includes risk assessments, policies and procedures governing interactions with government officials and business partners, due diligence on third-party agents and intermediaries, and regular training for employees in high-risk roles.
782	
783	**Whistleblower Program**
784	
785	We maintain a confidential ethics and compliance hotline, operated by an independent third-party provider, that enables employees and external stakeholders to report suspected violations of our Code of Conduct, policies, or applicable laws. Reports may be made anonymously where permitted by law. All reports are investigated promptly and thoroughly by our compliance team, and the Audit Committee receives quarterly summaries of hotline activity and investigation outcomes. Terraverde strictly prohibits retaliation against any individual who reports a concern in good faith.
786	
787	**Legal Counsel**
788	
789	Terraverde\'s legal department, in collaboration with our outside legal counsel at Pinehurst, Lowell & Gage LLP, provides guidance on compliance matters, regulatory developments, and legal risk management. Our legal team works closely with our EHS, sustainability, and compliance functions to ensure that our operations, disclosures, and business practices are conducted in accordance with applicable legal requirements.
790	
791	**5.3 Cybersecurity and Data Privacy**
792	
793	Terraverde recognizes the importance of protecting our information assets, operational technology systems, and stakeholder data from cybersecurity threats. As a manufacturer of specialty chemicals, our operations rely on a combination of information technology (IT) systems and operational technology (OT) systems, including process control systems, programmable logic controllers, and manufacturing execution systems.
794	
795	Our cybersecurity program is overseen by our Chief Information Officer and is managed by a dedicated information security team. The program is designed to identify, protect against, detect, respond to, and recover from cybersecurity threats, consistent with recognized frameworks such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
796	
797	Key elements of our cybersecurity governance include:
798	
799	> • Board-level oversight through the Audit Committee, which receives periodic briefings on cybersecurity risks, incidents, and program maturity
800	>
801	> • Annual cybersecurity risk assessments and penetration testing conducted by independent third-party security firms
802	>
803	> • Employee cybersecurity awareness training, including simulated phishing exercises
804	>
805	> • Incident response planning and tabletop exercises
806	>
807	> • Data privacy policies and practices governing the collection, use, and protection of employee and stakeholder personal information
808	
809	We are committed to maintaining the security and integrity of our information systems and to protecting the privacy of our stakeholders.
810

46	
47	8\. **Section 112 of the Clean Air Act, 42 U.S.C. § 7412**, directs the Administrator of EPA to promulgate regulations establishing emission standards for categories and subcategories of major sources and area sources of HAPs listed under Section 112(b) of the Act. These regulations, known as the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (\"NESHAPs\"), require the application of maximum achievable control technology (\"MACT\") for the control of HAP emissions from affected sources. Section 112 further requires owners and operators of affected sources to comply with all applicable emission standards, work practice standards, operational requirements, and monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements promulgated thereunder.
48	
49	9\. **40 C.F.R. Part 63, Subpart FFFF** --- National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing (\"MON\") --- establishes emission limitations, operating limits, and work practice standards for new and existing miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units. Subpart FFFF applies to major sources of HAP emissions that are engaged in the manufacture of miscellaneous organic chemicals, including but not limited to organic solvents, industrial adhesives, resins, and related specialty chemical products. Subpart FFFF includes specific requirements for process vents, storage tanks, wastewater, equipment leaks, heat exchange systems, and transfer operations, and establishes requirements for the installation and operation of emission control devices, continuous emission monitoring systems, and equipment leak detection and repair programs.
50	
51	10\. **LDAR Requirements Under Subpart FFFF.** Pursuant to 40 C.F.R. Part 63, Subpart FFFF, owners and operators of affected sources subject to equipment leak provisions must implement LDAR programs in accordance with the requirements cross-referenced from 40 C.F.R. Part 63, Subpart H (40 C.F.R. §§ 63.160 through 63.182). Subpart H requires that owners and operators conduct periodic monitoring of all regulated components, including pumps in light liquid service, valves in gas and vapor service and in light liquid service, connectors, agitators, compressors, pressure relief devices, and sampling connection systems, at specified frequencies using EPA Reference Method 21 (40 C.F.R. Part 60, Appendix A-7) or approved optical gas imaging (\"OGI\") technology in accordance with 40 C.F.R. § 63.180(b). Subpart H further requires that owners and operators maintain comprehensive records of all monitoring events, leak detections, repair actions, delay-of-repair justifications, and component identification information, and that leaking components be repaired within fifteen (15) calendar days of detection unless a delay-of-repair is documented in accordance with the applicable provisions of Subpart H.
52	
53	11\. **CEMS Requirements Under Subpart FFFF.** Pursuant to 40 C.F.R. Part 63, Subpart FFFF, owners and operators that employ thermal oxidizers, catalytic oxidizers, or other add-on emission control devices to achieve compliance with process vent emission limits must install, calibrate, maintain, and operate continuous emission monitoring systems (\"CEMS\") or continuous parameter monitoring systems (\"CPMS\") in accordance with the applicable performance specifications set forth in 40 C.F.R. Part 60, Appendix B, and the quality assurance procedures set forth in 40 C.F.R. Part 60, Appendix F. CEMS operators must maintain continuous, valid emissions data for a minimum of seventy-five percent (75%) of the operating hours in each reporting period, must conduct daily calibration drift checks, and must perform Relative Accuracy Test Audits (\"RATAs\") at least annually, as required under 40 C.F.R. Part 60, Appendix F, Section 5. Owners and operators must maintain complete records of all CEMS data, calibration events, RATA results, and any periods during which valid CEMS data was not available, including documentation of data substitution procedures employed during periods of CEMS malfunction or downtime.
54

This maximum penalty amount is subject to periodic adjustment for inflation in accordance with the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act Improvements Act of 2015 and EPA\'s implementing regulations at 40 C.F.R. Part 19.
56	
57	13\. **Section 113(e) of the Clean Air Act, 42 U.S.C. § 7413(e)**, directs that in determining the amount of any penalty to be assessed under Section 113, the Administrator shall take into consideration, in addition to such other factors as justice may require, the following: the size of the business, the economic impact of the penalty on the business, the violator\'s full compliance history and good faith efforts to comply, the duration of the violation as established by any credible evidence, the payment by the violator of penalties previously assessed for the same violation, the economic benefit of noncompliance, and the seriousness of the violation.

20	The regular meeting of the Board of Directors of Terraverde Holdings, Inc. was called to order at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time on Thursday, March 14, 2024, at the Company\'s principal executive offices located at 1200 Meridian Boulevard, Suite 800, Charlotte, NC 28203. A quorum was established, with all nine members of the Board present in person or by videoconference. Clara Whitfield, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary, served as Secretary of the meeting. Also present by invitation were Marcus Okonkwo, Vice President of Sustainability & Environmental Health and Safety; representatives of Pinehurst, Lowell & Gage LLP, including Sylvia Renard, Partner, and David Chu, Senior Associate; and Rebecca Tran, CPA, of Cresthaven Assurance Group, the Company\'s independent registered public accounting firm.

22	**Section 1.2 --- ESG Report Planning and Strategy**
23	
24	The Chair of the Board invited Marcus Okonkwo to present to the Board a proposal regarding the development and publication of the Company\'s first standalone Environmental, Social, and Governance report. Mr. Okonkwo began by noting that, to date, the Company had disclosed only limited environmental information in its Annual Report on Form 10-K, confined primarily to risk factor disclosures addressing potential environmental liabilities and regulatory compliance obligations. He observed that this approach, while consistent with historical practice, had become increasingly insufficient in light of evolving investor expectations, regulatory requirements, and the growing importance of sustainability reporting to capital markets participants.
25	
26	Mr. Okonkwo recommended that the Company publish an inaugural standalone ESG and sustainability report for fiscal year 2024. He proposed that the report be aligned with the International Sustainability Standards Board\'s IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures standard, as well as the SEC\'s climate disclosure rules adopted in March 2024. He noted that the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) framework, which underpins both ISSB S2 and the SEC rules, would serve as an organizing principle for the climate-related content of the report. Mr. Okonkwo further proposed that the report cover a broad range of topics beyond climate, including water stewardship, waste management, occupational health and safety, workforce diversity and inclusion, and corporate governance practices.
27	
28	The Chair of the Audit Committee expressed strong support for the proposal. She noted that institutional investors, including several of the Company\'s largest shareholders, had been pressing for more comprehensive and standardized ESG disclosures. She referenced recent feedback from Ridgeline Capital Markets, the Company\'s investment bank, which had indicated that the absence of a standalone sustainability report and the Company\'s relatively low ESG ratings from major rating agencies were likely contributing to a valuation discount relative to peers and could incrementally affect the Company\'s cost of capital over time. The Audit Committee Chair stated that a well-prepared, credible ESG report would be responsive to these concerns.
29	
30	Mr. Okonkwo reported that the Company had retained Granville Analytics, LLC, based in Austin, Texas, to assist with the development of the greenhouse gas emissions inventory and the calculation of Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 emissions. He stated that the engagement was being led by Dr. Priya Nair, the firm\'s Managing Director and a recognized expert in corporate GHG accounting. Granville Analytics had already commenced work on the baseline year GHG inventory using 2023 operational data from the Company\'s six manufacturing facilities and its Charlotte headquarters. Mr. Okonkwo proposed a target publication date of April 30, 2025, for the report, which would be posted on the Company\'s investor relations website and potentially filed as an exhibit to an amended Annual Report on Form 10-K/A.
31	
32	David Chu of Pinehurst, Lowell & Gage LLP then addressed the Board regarding the legal implications of the proposed ESG report. Mr. Chu advised the Board that if the ESG report were filed with the SEC as an exhibit to the 10-K or 10-K/A, all statements contained therein would be subject to securities law liability, including the anti-fraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 promulgated thereunder. He noted that even if the report were published only on the Company\'s website without being incorporated by reference into SEC filings, it could still be cited by plaintiffs in securities fraud litigation as evidence of materially misleading statements or omissions. Mr. Chu therefore recommended a thorough legal review of the near-final draft of the report prior to publication. Clara Whitfield confirmed that she would engage Pinehurst, Lowell & Gage LLP to conduct a comprehensive \"cold eyes\" review of the near-final draft of the ESG report and that the firm\'s review would encompass factual accuracy, legal compliance, and consistency with the Company\'s SEC filings and other public disclosures.
33	
34	Following discussion, the Board unanimously approved the proposal to proceed with the development and publication of the Company\'s inaugural FY2024 ESG and sustainability report. The Board directed management to coordinate with Granville Analytics, LLC for the GHG inventory and emissions calculations and with Pinehurst, Lowell & Gage LLP for legal review. The Board further authorized Ms. Whitfield to formally engage Pinehurst, Lowell & Gage LLP for the pre-publication review on terms to be agreed.

42	**Section 1.4 --- Environmental Compliance Update**
43	
44	Clara Whitfield provided a brief update on a pending environmental enforcement matter involving the Company\'s manufacturing facility in Savannah, Georgia, located at 2100 Port Wentworth Highway, Savannah, GA 31407. Ms. Whitfield reported that from October 3 through October 5, 2023, the United States Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, conducted an on-site compliance inspection of the Savannah facility pursuant to its authority under Section 114 of the Clean Air Act, 42 U.S.C. Section 7414. During the inspection, EPA personnel identified potential violations of Clean Air Act Section 112 requirements related to the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP), specifically under 40 CFR Part 63, Subpart FFFF.
45	
46	Ms. Whitfield reported that the potential violations identified by EPA during the inspection related to two principal areas: first, the facility\'s failure to conduct required leak detection and repair (LDAR) monitoring at the frequency specified under Subpart FFFF; and second, improper recordkeeping of continuous emissions monitoring system (CEMS) data for two thermal oxidizer units designated as TO-301 and TO-302. Ms. Whitfield noted that the Company had received written correspondence from EPA Region 4 summarizing the inspection findings and requesting the Company\'s response, but that no formal enforcement action, administrative order, or penalty assessment had been filed as of the date of the meeting.
47	
48	Ms. Whitfield further reported that the Company had retained Fieldstone & Hale LLP, an environmental litigation firm with offices in Atlanta, Georgia, and Washington, D.C., to represent the Company in connection with the EPA matter. The engagement was being led by Jonathan Stroud, the firm\'s managing partner and a former senior enforcement attorney with EPA Region 4. Mr. Stroud and his team were in the process of reviewing the inspection findings and preparing the Company\'s response to EPA.
49	
50	The Board directed management to cooperate fully with EPA Region 4 in the investigation, to continue to work with Fieldstone & Hale LLP to address the identified issues, and to keep the Board informed of any material developments in the matter, including any proposed penalty or enforcement action.

68	The Chair of the Board invited Jonathan Stroud of Fieldstone & Hale LLP to provide a detailed update on the EPA enforcement matter involving the Company\'s Savannah, Georgia manufacturing facility, which had been previously discussed at the March 14, 2024 Board meeting.

70	Mr. Stroud reported that on June 14, 2024, EPA Region 4 issued Administrative Consent Order No. CAA-04-2024-3187 against Terraverde Holdings, Inc. in connection with the Savannah, GA facility located at 2100 Port Wentworth Highway, Savannah, GA 31407. The Consent Order was issued pursuant to Section 113(a)(1) and Section 113(d) of the Clean Air Act, 42 U.S.C. Sections 7413(a)(1) and 7413(d), and was based on the Clean Air Act Section 112 (NESHAP) violations identified during EPA\'s October 3-5, 2023 on-site inspection. 71	
72	> \(a\) Failure to conduct required leak detection and repair (LDAR) monitoring at the frequency required by 40 CFR Part 63, Subpart FFFF, resulting in multiple missed monitoring cycles at equipment components subject to the LDAR program at the Savannah facility; and
73	>
74	> \(b\) Improper recordkeeping of continuous emissions monitoring system (CEMS) data for thermal oxidizer units designated as TO-301 and TO-302, including gaps in recorded data, failure to document calibration drift checks, and failure to maintain CEMS quality assurance records in accordance with applicable requirements under 40 CFR Part 63, Subpart FFFF and the facility\'s Title V operating permit.
75	
76	Mr. Stroud then summarized the principal terms and financial obligations set forth in the Consent Order:
77	
78	> • **Administrative Penalty:** \$1,175,000, payable to the United States Treasury within sixty (60) days of the effective date of the Consent Order.
79	>
80	> • **Supplemental Environmental Project (SEP):** \$425,000 investment in a community air quality monitoring initiative in Chatham County, Georgia, to be implemented in coordination with the Chatham County Health Department. The SEP required the installation and operation of three ambient air quality monitoring stations in communities adjacent to the Port Wentworth industrial corridor.
81	>
82	> • **Total Financial Obligation:** \$1,600,000 (consisting of the \$1,175,000 penalty and the \$425,000 SEP commitment).
83	>
84	> • **Corrective Action Requirements:** (i) Complete upgrades to the LDAR program at the Savannah facility, including implementation of enhanced monitoring schedules and installation of optical gas imaging (OGI) technology, by March 31, 2025; and (ii) complete an independent third-party audit of CEMS data integrity for thermal oxidizers TO-301 and TO-302 by June 30, 2025, with audit results to be submitted to EPA Region 4 within thirty (30) days of completion.

He noted that the \$1,175,000 penalty was within the range previously anticipated by Fieldstone & Hale based on their analysis of comparable enforcement actions and EPA\'s penalty policy guidelines. Mr. Stroud further noted that contested proceedings before the EPA Environmental Appeals Board would be costly, protracted, and unlikely to result in a materially lower penalty.
87	
88	Clara Whitfield reported to the Board that the Company had executed the Consent Order on July 8, 2024, as previously authorized by the Board pursuant to a resolution adopted in executive session at a special meeting held on June 28, 2024. She confirmed that the sixty-day payment deadline for the \$1,175,000 penalty would fall on approximately September 6, 2024.

118	**Section 3.2 --- GHG Emissions Reduction Targets --- Presentation and Approval**
119	
120	The Chair of the Board stated that the principal purpose of the special meeting was to consider and approve proposed greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets for the Company, as recommended by management and supported by the feasibility analysis prepared by Granville Analytics, LLC.
121	
122	Marcus Okonkwo presented the proposed targets, noting that they had been developed in consultation with Dr. Priya Nair and her team at Granville Analytics over the preceding several months. Mr. Okonkwo stated that the targets reflected a balance between ambition and achievability, consistent with the Company\'s operational profile, capital investment plans, and available decarbonization pathways. He presented the following proposed targets for Board consideration:
123	
124	> • **Near-Term Target (2030):** A 30% reduction in combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 (market-based) greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, measured against a 2023 baseline of 401,250 metric tons CO2e. The corresponding 2030 target level would be 280,875 metric tons CO2e (calculated as 401,250 multiplied by 0.70).
125	>
126	> • **Long-Term Target (2050):** Net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Mr. Okonkwo characterized this target as aspirational and noted that it had not yet been submitted to the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) for validation.
127	
128	Dr. Priya Nair then addressed the Board regarding the methodology underlying the targets and the feasibility of achieving them. Dr. Nair explained that the 30% reduction target by 2030 was achievable through a combination of identified and planned measures, including energy efficiency investments across the Company\'s manufacturing facilities, fuel switching from natural gas to lower-carbon alternatives at certain facilities where technically and economically feasible, and increased procurement of renewable energy through power purchase agreements and the purchase of renewable energy certificates (RECs). She noted that the Company had already begun purchasing RECs to reduce its Scope 2 (market-based) emissions and that management had identified several additional capital projects that, if implemented on the anticipated timeline, would contribute meaningfully to emissions reductions. Dr. Nair presented a preliminary decarbonization pathway analysis showing projected year-by-year emissions reductions under various scenarios.
129	
130	The representative of Ridgeline Capital Markets addressed the Board regarding the capital markets implications of setting credible GHG reduction targets. The Ridgeline representative observed that the establishment of quantitative, time-bound emissions reduction targets, particularly when supported by a credible methodology and a clear implementation roadmap, could improve the Company\'s ESG ratings from major agencies and, over time, potentially lower the Company\'s cost of capital by broadening its appeal to ESG-focused institutional investors.
131	
132	Discussion ensued regarding the 2050 net-zero target. Several directors noted that the 2050 timeline extended well beyond the Company\'s current strategic planning horizon and that significant uncertainties existed regarding the technologies, costs, and market conditions that would prevail over such a timeframe. The directors agreed that the 2050 net-zero target should be clearly characterized as an aspirational, long-term goal subject to review and adjustment as circumstances evolved. Clara Whitfield advised that any public disclosure of forward-looking targets, including both the 2030 and 2050 targets, should be accompanied by appropriate cautionary language, including safe harbor statements under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, to the extent applicable.
133	
134	Following further discussion, the Board unanimously approved the GHG emissions reduction targets as presented by Mr. Okonkwo on September 12, 2024, including the 30% reduction by 2030 (to 280,875 metric tons CO2e from the 2023 baseline of 401,250 metric tons CO2e) and the aspirational net-zero by 2050 target.

The NOV alleged that the facility had exceeded permitted limits for Total Suspended Solids (TSS) in stormwater discharges from the facility\'s industrial stormwater outfall, in violation of the facility\'s NPDES General Permit for Industrial Stormwater.
211	
212	Mr. Okonkwo explained that the TSS exceedances were related to a construction project being conducted by a third-party contractor on a parcel adjacent to the facility\'s stormwater outfall. The construction activity had generated significant sediment that migrated into the facility\'s stormwater conveyance system. Mr. Okonkwo reported that the Company had implemented remedial measures promptly upon identifying the issue, including the installation of silt fencing, construction of temporary settling basins, and coordination with the third-party contractor to implement additional best management practices to control sediment runoff.
213	
214	Mr. Okonkwo further stated that no penalty had been assessed by ADEM in connection with the NOV and that the Company was in discussions with ADEM to resolve the matter informally. He expressed the view that the remedial measures implemented to date, combined with the Company\'s cooperation with ADEM, would support a favorable resolution.
215	
216	Clara Whitfield advised the Board that, while no monetary penalty had been assessed, the NOV constituted a pending environmental enforcement matter that arose within the FY2024 reporting period. She stated that the NOV should be disclosed in the Company\'s ESG report as an environmental compliance matter, consistent with the Company\'s commitment to transparent and comprehensive reporting. Ms. Whitfield directed Mr. Okonkwo to include appropriate language regarding the ADEM NOV in the draft ESG report, noting the nature of the violation, the remedial actions taken, and the current status of discussions with ADEM.
217	
218	The Board directed management to continue working cooperatively with ADEM toward resolution of the matter and to keep the Board informed of any material developments, including any penalty assessment or formal enforcement action.
219	
220	**Section 4.6 --- ESG Report --- Status and Preliminary Data Review**
221	
222	Marcus Okonkwo presented a comprehensive status update on the Company\'s FY2024 ESG and sustainability report. He reported that Granville Analytics, LLC had completed the FY2024 greenhouse gas emissions inventory. Mr. Okonkwo presented the following preliminary GHG emissions figures to the Board, which had been calculated and confirmed by Dr. Priya Nair\'s team at Granville Analytics using the operational control consolidation approach under the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard:
223	
224	  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
225	  **Emissions Category**                         **Metric Tons CO2e**
226	  ---------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
227	  Total Scope 1 Emissions                        265,030
228	
229	  Total Scope 2 Emissions (Market-Based)         118,790
230	
231	  Total Scope 2 Emissions (Location-Based)       126,340
232	
233	  **Combined Scope 1 + 2 (Market-Based)**        **383,820**
234	
235	  Total Scope 3 (Categories 1, 3, 4, 6, 9, 11)   615,600
236	  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
237	
238	Mr. Okonkwo noted that the combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 (market-based) figure of 383,820 metric tons CO2e represented a reduction of approximately 4.3% from the 2023 baseline of 401,250 metric tons CO2e. He stated that this was a positive initial step in the Company\'s decarbonization journey, reflecting the early impact of energy efficiency measures and renewable energy certificate (REC) procurement. However, he acknowledged candidly that the rate of reduction would need to accelerate significantly in future years for the Company to achieve its Board-approved target of a 30% reduction by 2030 (to 280,875 metric tons CO2e). Dr. Nair and her team at Granville Analytics had verified and confirmed the accuracy of all figures presented.
239	
240	Clara Whitfield asked Mr. Okonkwo about the planned alignment of the ESG report with the ISSB S2 Climate-related Disclosures standard and the SEC\'s climate disclosure rules. Mr. Okonkwo confirmed that the report was being structured to follow those frameworks and that the climate-related disclosures in the report would address governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets, consistent with the four-pillar structure of ISSB S2 and the TCFD framework. Ms. Whitfield noted the importance of presenting both market-based and location-based Scope 2 emissions figures in the report, as required by the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance and as incorporated into the ISSB S2 disclosure requirements. She directed that the report clearly present both figures with appropriate explanatory context.
241	
242	Mr. Okonkwo then presented additional environmental, health, and safety data to the Board for the FY2024 reporting period:
243	
244	> • **Water:** Total water withdrawal for FY2024 was 847 million gallons, of which 612 million gallons were drawn from municipal water supply sources and 235 million gallons from groundwater sources.
245	>
246	> • **Hazardous Waste:** Total hazardous waste generated was 14,820 metric tons. Of that total, 3,410 metric tons (23.0%) were recycled or reclaimed; the balance was treated and disposed of through permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facilities.
247	>
248	> • **Non-Hazardous Waste:** Total non-hazardous solid waste generated was 41,670 metric tons. Of that total, 22,090 metric tons (53.0%) were diverted from landfill through recycling, composting, and beneficial reuse programs.
249	>
250	> • **Safety:** The Company\'s Total Recordable Incident Rate (TRIR) for FY2024 was 1.82 per 200,000 hours worked, based on 52 total recordable incidents and approximately 5,762,000 hours worked during the year. The Days Away, Restricted, or Transferred (DART) rate was 0.91. There were zero work-related fatalities during FY2024.
251	
252	Mr. Okonkwo stated that the draft ESG report would bear a cover date of March 15, 2025, and that the Company was targeting a publication date of April 30, 2025, consistent with the timeline originally approved by the Board at the March 14, 2024 meeting. He noted that upon completion of the draft, it would be circulated to Pinehurst, Lowell & Gage LLP for the comprehensive \"cold eyes\" legal review that Ms. Whitfield had previously arranged. Mr. Okonkwo stated he expected the draft to be ready for PL&G\'s review by mid-February 2025.
253	
254	**Section 4.7 --- Other Business**
255	
256	The Board briefly discussed several routine matters. The Chair of the Compensation Committee provided a summary update regarding executive compensation planning for FY2025, noting that the committee was on track to present its recommendations at the next regularly scheduled meeting. Clara Whitfield provided a preliminary timeline for planning for the Company\'s 2025 Annual Meeting of Stockholders, expected to be held in May 2025. There was also a brief discussion regarding the Company\'s ongoing engagement with Ridgeline Capital Markets concerning investor perception, ESG-related shareholder engagement, and the Company\'s positioning relative to peer companies in ESG rating frameworks. No formal action was required on any of these matters.
257	
258	**Section 4.8 --- Adjournment**
259	
260	There being no further business to come before the Board, the meeting was adjourned at 1:00 p.m. Eastern Time upon a motion duly made, seconded, and unanimously carried.
261	
262	**[AUTHENTICATION AND CERTIFICATION]{.underline}**
263	
264	I, Clara Whitfield, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of Terraverde Holdings, Inc., hereby certify that the foregoing are true and correct excerpts from the minutes of the meetings of the Board of Directors of Terraverde Holdings, Inc. held on March 14, 2024, July 18, 2024, September 12, 2024, and December 12, 2024. These excerpts have been prepared for the purpose of the pre-publication legal review of the Company\'s FY2024 ESG/Sustainability Report by Pinehurst, Lowell & Gage LLP.
265

def issue(num, sev, title, draft, evidence, risk, fix):

issue(1,"Critical","Environmental compliance record misstated; EPA Consent Order omitted",
 "Section 3.3.1: \"In FY2024, Terraverde received no material environmental penalties or sanctions. Our EHS management system ensures ongoing monitoring and compliance across all manufacturing facilities, and our compliance teams work proactively to identify and address potential issues before they rise to the level of regulatory enforcement.\" CEO Letter: \"We are proud that our environmental compliance record reflects our commitment to operating responsibly. We hold ourselves to the highest standards of regulatory compliance . . . .\"",
 "EPA Region 4 issued Administrative Consent Order No. CAA-04-2024-3187 on June 14, 2024 (effective July 8, 2024) for the Savannah facility. The Order assessed a $1,175,000 civil penalty and required a $425,000 SEP, for a $1,600,000 total obligation (Consent Order paras. 34, 37, 45, 55). It made findings on four counts of CAA Section 112/NESHAP Subpart FFFF violations: LDAR monitoring frequency (412 and 387 unmonitored components; 56 new components not monitored), late repairs (23 leaking components), CEMS data integrity (TO-301 data gaps of 21% and 15% of operating hours; no 2022 RATAs) and recordkeeping. The violations ran for about 22 months and were found by EPA inspection, not self-identified. Minutes: on July 18, 2024 the GC said the Order is \"a significant environmental enforcement action\" to be disclosed in the 10-K and is relevant to ESG disclosures. D. Chu\x27s memorandum of July 5, 2024 advised that an ESG report \"that asserts the absence of material environmental penalties without disclosing the Consent Order could be viewed as materially misleading.\" The Board directed disclosure \"in all relevant filings, reports, and disclosures, including the forthcoming ESG report\" and the GC repeated this on December 12, 2024. The Email Chain (Okonkwo, March 11, 2025) confirms the Order \"was disclosed in the 10-K\" and that the compliance section was drafted to say \"no material penalties\"; the email asks whether to revisit, and no answer appears.",
 "This is an affirmative misstatement and a half-truth on a topic the Draft itself identifies as a priority material topic (\"Environmental compliance\", Section 3.1). A penalty of more than $1 million is above the $300,000 (or up to $1 million if the issuer elects) threshold for environmental proceedings with a governmental authority under Regulation S-K Item 103(c)(3)(iii), which is why it appears in the 10-K. A statement that directly contradicts the Company\x27s own 10-K, made after written advice of counsel and Board direction to the contrary, presents strong Rule 10b-5 risk, including scienter, and Section 18 risk if the report is filed. Characterizing the penalty as \"not material\" is not a defense: the statement is qualitative (compliance record), the Order is a matter of public record (paras. 70-71), and an ESG audience treats enforcement history as material regardless of its size relative to revenue. The statement that teams address issues \"before they rise to the level of regulatory enforcement\" is contradicted by the EPA inspection findings. The CEO letter compounds the problem, and similar \"puffery\" has been held actionable when contradicted by known, specific facts.",
 "Delete the \"no material environmental penalties\" sentence and the \"before they rise to the level of regulatory enforcement\" clause. Add a subsection along these lines: \"Savannah, Georgia Consent Order. On June 14, 2024, EPA Region 4 issued an Administrative Consent Order and Agreement (Docket No. CAA-04-2024-3187), effective July 8, 2024, resolving alleged violations of the Clean Air Act NESHAP for Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing (40 C.F.R. Part 63, Subpart FFFF) identified during an October 2023 EPA inspection of our Savannah facility, relating to leak detection and repair monitoring and repair, continuous emission monitoring data and recordkeeping. Without admitting or denying EPA\x27s findings, we paid a civil penalty of $1,175,000 and agreed to fund a $425,000 Supplemental Environmental Project for community air quality monitoring in Chatham County, Georgia, and to complete LDAR program upgrades and an independent CEMS data integrity audit. [Insert status as of publication.]\" Revise the CEO letter to remove \"compliance record\" and \"highest standards\" language, or tie it to the Order (for example, \"FY2024 reinforced the importance of rigorous compliance; we resolved an EPA enforcement matter at our Savannah facility and are investing in program upgrades . . .\"). Conform the Section 3.3.1 language to the 10-K Item 103 disclosure verbatim where possible.")

issue(2,"Critical","Superfund / legacy contamination exposure denied",
 "Section 3.3.2: \"Terraverde has no material exposure to legacy contamination or Superfund liabilities. Our manufacturing facilities are located on relatively modern industrial sites, and we have not inherited significant environmental legacies from prior operations or previous site occupants.\"",
 "Minutes (July 18, 2024, Section 2.3): the Company has been \"formally identified as a potentially responsible party (PRP) under CERCLA\" at the Crowley Landfill Superfund Site, Aiken County, SC (RI/FS phase, EPA Region 4), for disposal of process waste from about 1987 to 1995. Its estimated allocated share is about $3.8 million, and the Board approved recording a $3.8 million ASC 450 reserve (\"probable and reasonably estimable\"), which Cresthaven confirmed. Reaffirmed on September 12, 2024 (Section 3.3), with a warning that the share \"could change as the RI/FS progressed.\"",
 "The statement is flatly false. It also conflicts with the audited financial statements, which carry a recorded environmental reserve (and presumably related contingency disclosure in the 10-K). The \"relatively modern sites\" framing is misleading because CERCLA liability here comes from off-site disposal (arranger liability under 42 U.S.C. Section 9607(a)(3)), not from the condition of current sites. Joint and several liability under CERCLA, the early RI/FS stage and the possibility of reallocation mean the exposure could grow. Denying any Superfund exposure while a reserve is booked is a classic inconsistency that plaintiffs use in Rule 10b-5 complaints.",
 "Replace the first two sentences with accurate disclosure, for example: \"Terraverde has been named a potentially responsible party under CERCLA at the Crowley Landfill Superfund Site in Aiken County, South Carolina, relating to the historical off-site disposal of process wastes between approximately 1987 and 1995. The site is in the remedial investigation/feasibility study phase. We have recorded an environmental reserve of $3.8 million, representing our estimated allocated share of remediation costs; this estimate may change as the RI/FS progresses.\" Conform to the 10-K contingencies note and confirm with Cresthaven and Fieldstone & Hale. Check whether the soil and groundwater monitoring statement in the next paragraph (\"results . . . have not indicated contamination requiring significant remediation\") can be substantiated for every site.")

issue(4,"Critical","Progress-to-target overstated (6.2% vs. 4.34%)",
 "Section 3.2.4: \"379,820 metric tons CO2e, representing a 6.2% reduction from our 2023 baseline of 401,250\" and \"we are encouraged by this initial progress\"; Section 6.1: \"FY2024 Progress vs. 2023 Baseline: 6.2%.\"",
 "Correct calculation: (401,250 - 383,820) / 401,250 = 4.34% (Workbook Summary, \"YoY Reduction vs. 2023 Baseline 4.34%\"). Even using the Draft\x27s own erroneous 379,820, the reduction is 5.34%, not 6.2%; we found no data set that produces 6.2%. The Board was told on December 12, 2024 that the reduction was \"approximately 4.3%,\" and Mr. Okonkwo said then that \"the rate of reduction would need to accelerate significantly.\" In the Email Chain, Mr. Okonkwo proposed 6.2% and asked whether the GC was \"comfortable . . . given this will be in a document filed with the SEC\"; Dr. Nair flagged that the total was unverified; the GC replied \"6.2% is a good number . . . Let\x27s put our best foot forward.\"",
 "This is the single most prominent quantitative claim in the climate section, and it overstates progress by about 43% (6.2 vs. 4.34). The record shows the Board and management knew the correct figure was about 4.3%, and that the GC approved 6.2% after being told it was unverified. That chronology would be powerful scienter evidence in a Rule 10b-5 action and is the kind of misstatement the SEC Enforcement Division has pursued in ESG cases. Separately, attributing the reduction to \"operational efficiency measures\" is unsupported: much of the change comes from REC purchases (Issue 6).",
 "Replace with: \"Our FY2024 combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 (market-based) emissions were 383,820 mt CO2e, approximately 4.3% below our 2023 baseline of 401,250 mt CO2e. On a location-based basis, combined emissions were 391,370 mt CO2e [approximately 2.5% below the baseline - confirm baseline basis]. A substantial portion of the market-based reduction reflects the purchase of unbundled RECs. Meeting our 2030 target of 280,875 mt CO2e will require an additional reduction of approximately 102,945 mt CO2e (about 27% below FY2024 levels), and the pace of reduction must accelerate significantly.\" Recommend that the GC formally withdraw the March 11, 2025 direction in writing and that the decision be documented, given that the existing email record is discoverable.")

issue(5,"Critical","Renewable energy claim (\"transitioned 40% ... to renewable sources\")",
 "Section 3.2.5: \"Terraverde has transitioned 40% of its electricity consumption to renewable sources through the purchase of renewable energy certificates (RECs).\" Section 6.1: \"Renewable Energy as % of Total Electricity: 40%.\" Section 3.2.1: Scope 2 reflects \"the specific contractual instruments in place for electricity procurement at each facility.\" Section 3.2.5 also says the RECs are \"exclusively claimed by Terraverde.\"",
 "Workbook REC Purchases tab: four purchases from Northshore Energy Advisors totaling 119,680 MWh (40.0% of 299,200 MWh consumed), all \"Unbundled national RECs; not facility-specific; not from a PPA or on-site generation\"; \"No Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) or on-site renewable generation in place.\" Dr. Nair (March 10, 2025) warned that \"transitioned . . . to renewable sources\" \"could reasonably be read as implying that Terraverde has physically changed its electricity supply,\" noted SEC, FTC and plaintiff-bar scrutiny, and proposed: \"Terraverde has procured renewable energy certificates (RECs) covering approximately 40% of its total electricity consumption.\" The GC nevertheless approved the stronger language on March 11, 2025, citing Ridgeline\x27s view that investors \"respond much more positively\" to affirmative claims.",
 "The claim implies a physical or contractual change in electricity supply that has not occurred; Terraverde\x27s facilities still draw 100% grid power from Southeastern utilities. The Email Chain shows the language was chosen for its investor appeal over the consultant\x27s express warning, which increases Rule 10b-5 risk and the risk of an SEC greenwashing inquiry. The FTC Green Guides (16 C.F.R. Section 260.15) require renewable energy claims to be qualified so they do not mislead and to make clear the role of RECs; state consumer protection and anti-greenwashing claims (and NGO complaints) are also possible. Describing the RECs as \"specific contractual instruments . . . at each facility\" is inaccurate because they are national and not facility-specific. \"Renewable energy as % of total electricity: 40%\" in Table 6.1 repeats the problem.",
 "Adopt Granville\x27s language or similar: \"In FY2024, Terraverde purchased and retired Green-e Energy certified, unbundled renewable energy certificates (RECs) equal to approximately 40% of our total electricity consumption (119,680 MWh). These RECs are sourced from wind and solar projects located across the United States, are not associated with a power purchase agreement or on-site generation, and do not change the physical electricity delivered to our facilities. We apply them in calculating our market-based Scope 2 emissions.\" Rename the 6.1 line to \"Electricity consumption matched by unbundled RECs (%)\". Delete \"specific contractual instruments in place . . . at each facility\". Also remove \"transitioned\" from any CEO, investor or marketing material.")

issue(6,"High","Location-based Scope 2 omitted; progress is mostly REC-driven",
 "Sections 3.2.1, 3.2.3 and 6.1 present only market-based Scope 2 (118,790). The Draft says it follows the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance and \"referenced\" IFRS S2.",
 "Workbook: location-based Scope 2 = 126,340 mt (eGRID 2023); combined location-based 391,370. Minutes (December 12, 2024): the GC \"directed that the report clearly present both figures with appropriate explanatory context,\" noting dual reporting is required by the Scope 2 Guidance and IFRS S2.",
 "The GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance requires dual reporting (location- and market-based) for companies operating in markets with contractual instruments. IFRS S2 requires location-based Scope 2 plus information about contractual instruments. Leaving out location-based figures while claiming to follow these standards is misleading, and it hides that REC purchases account for much of the market-based improvement. On a location-based basis, the year-over-year change in combined emissions is only about 2.5% (if the 2023 baseline had no REC benefit). It also contradicts the GC\x27s express direction.",
 "Add location-based Scope 2 (facility table and totals), combined location-based Scope 1+2 (391,370) and narrative explaining the difference. State whether the 2023 baseline includes any REC benefit and whether the target is measured market-based only (it is). Consider disclosing progress on both bases.")

issue(8,"High","LDAR and compliance-system claims contradicted; Consent Order compliance status and term discrepancies",
 "Section 3.2.2: \"we have implemented leak detection and repair (LDAR) programs at all manufacturing facilities to minimize these losses.\" Section 3.3.1: \"Our EHS management system ensures ongoing monitoring and compliance across all manufacturing facilities.\" Neither section describes the Order\x27s corrective-action obligations.",
 "The Consent Order makes LDAR failures at Savannah the basis of Counts I and II and requires: (a) a digital barcode/RFID component tracking system, personnel retraining, a full baseline survey and an independent third-party LDAR audit by a firm not previously retained, all by March 31, 2025, with officer certification within 15 days (paras. 46-48); (b) an independent CEMS data integrity audit with the final report to EPA by June 30, 2025, and implementation of recommendations within 60 days (paras. 49-51); (c) quarterly compliance reports starting 90 days after July 8, 2024 (para. 52); (d) a SEP Implementation Plan within 60 days of the effective date (para. 40), four monitoring stations (para. 38) operated for five years, and semi-annual SEP progress reports starting six months after the effective date (para. 43); and (e) penalty payment within 30 days of the effective date (para. 36), i.e., by about August 7, 2024. Stipulated penalties apply (para. 63: $2,500/day for LDAR or CEMS deadlines; $1,000/day for late reports or payment; $5,000/day for SEP delay). The Minutes describe the Order differently: a 60-day payment period (due about September 6, 2024), three monitoring stations, LDAR upgrades consisting of \"enhanced monitoring schedules and installation of optical gas imaging (OGI),\" and CEMS audit results due within 30 days of completion. On December 12, 2024, LDAR upgrades were about 60% complete, the SEP had \"not yet commenced\" and the SEP vendor was not yet selected. The penalty was paid \"in August 2024\" (exact date not stated).",
 "The Draft\x27s general claims about LDAR and compliance systems are misleading in light of the Order. More importantly, the Minutes suggest management may be working from an inaccurate understanding of the Order: wrong payment period, wrong number of SEP stations, and LDAR scope that omits the digital tracking system, third-party audit and baseline survey. That creates a real risk of missed deadlines and stipulated penalties: (i) the payment may have been late if made after about August 7, 2024; (ii) the SEP Implementation Plan was due about September 6, 2024, but no vendor had been selected by December; (iii) the March 31, 2025 LDAR deadline falls two weeks after the Draft\x27s cover date. Any new deviation would also undercut the ESG narrative and may require disclosure.",
 "(1) Revise Section 3.2.2 to say, for example, \"we maintain LDAR programs at our manufacturing facilities and, at our Savannah facility, are completing upgrades required under a 2024 EPA consent order.\" (2) Delete or qualify \"ensures ongoing monitoring and compliance.\" (3) In the Consent Order disclosure (Issue 1), state the status of each corrective action as of publication. (4) Separately, ask Fieldstone & Hale to confirm promptly: the penalty payment date; whether the SEP Implementation Plan and semi-annual SEP reports were submitted on time and whether EPA approved the plan; whether quarterly compliance reports have been filed; whether the LDAR scope being implemented matches para. 46 (digital tracking, retraining, independent auditor, baseline survey); and whether the March 31, 2025 certification will be timely. Correct the Board\x27s understanding of the Order terms in the next Board materials.")

issue(9,"High","Filing the report as an exhibit to Form 10-K/A",
 "Sections 2.3 and 7: the report \"will be filed as an exhibit to the company\x27s Annual Report on Form 10-K/A.\" Section 5.1: the Board \"authorized its planned publication and SEC filing.\"",
 "Minutes (March 14, 2024): D. Chu advised that filing would subject every statement to securities-law liability; Mr. Okonkwo described filing only as \"potentially\" occurring. No Minutes excerpt records Board authorization to file. The Email Chain treats filing as decided.",
 "Filing (rather than posting on the website) makes the report part of an Exchange Act report. That creates Section 18 liability and exposure to SEC enforcement for filed-document accuracy, brings it within the CEO/CFO certifications required by Rules 13a-14(a)/(b) (SOX Sections 302 and 906) for the 10-K/A and disclosure-controls evaluation, and may cause it to be incorporated by reference into Securities Act registration statements (e.g., Form S-3/S-8). That would raise Section 11 exposure and expert-consent questions (see Issue 25). The report contains forward-looking targets, estimates (spend-based Scope 3) and unassured data, none of which have been through the disclosure controls applied to the 10-K. There is no apparent legal requirement to file it, and the SEC climate rule is stayed (Issue 11).",
 "Strongly recommend not filing the report with the SEC. Publish it on the website with a clear statement that it is not incorporated by reference into any SEC filing, and with robust cautionary language. If the Company nonetheless wishes to file it, (i) obtain express Board (or Audit Committee) authorization; (ii) subject the report to full disclosure-controls procedures and officer sub-certifications; (iii) consider furnishing rather than filing where permitted; and (iv) remove the auditor reference or obtain consent. Correct the Section 5.1 description either way.")

issue(10,"High","No forward-looking statements / cautionary language",
 "The CEO Letter, Sections 3.2.4, 3.2.5 and 3.4-3.5 contain targets (30% by 2030; net-zero by 2050), a planned $45 million capital program (2025-2028), PPA and on-site solar plans, \"intend to significantly expand\" renewable energy and future assurance plans. Climate targets have been a focus of SEC comment letters and private litigation. The CEO letter\x27s \"we have set ambitious goals\" and \"to achieve these targets, we plan to invest approximately $45 million\" will be read as commitments.",
 "Add a prominent forward-looking statements section, at the front or end of the report and referenced in the CEO letter, that identifies the targets, capex, PPAs and Scope 3 refinements as forward-looking. It should list specific risk factors (technology availability and cost, utility grid mix, REC market, regulatory changes, capital allocation, production growth, data and methodology changes and baseline recalculation, consent order compliance) and cross-reference the 10-K risk factors. Add a methodology and estimates disclaimer (Scope 3 spend-based estimates, data quality ratings, unassured data). Describe the 2050 net-zero goal consistently as aspirational everywhere (the CEO letter is reasonably careful; Section 5.1 calls it an \"aspiration\" but approved as a \"target\").")

issue(11,"High","Framework alignment claims overstated; reference to SEC climate rules",
 "Sections 2.3 and 7 list \"U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission climate disclosure rules\" and say the Company has \"considered the SEC\x27s climate-related disclosure requirements\"; the report claims to reference IFRS S2 and to follow the GHG Protocol standards.",
 "Minutes (March 14 and December 12, 2024): the report was to be aligned with ISSB S2 and the SEC rules \"adopted in March 2024,\" covering all four TCFD pillars.",
 "The SEC\x27s climate disclosure rules (Release No. 33-11275, March 6, 2024) were voluntarily stayed by the SEC in April 2024 pending Eighth Circuit review. The Commission subsequently voted (March 2025) to end its defense of the rules, so they are not in effect and no compliance obligation has arisen. Listing them as a framework suggests a level of compliance the Draft does not provide and may soon look outdated. The Draft also falls short of IFRS S2 in material respects: no location-based Scope 2; no climate scenario analysis or resilience assessment; limited description of climate-related risks and opportunities and their current and anticipated financial effects; no transition plan detail beyond a capex figure; no internal carbon price or remuneration linkage disclosure; and Scope 3 without category-by-category rationale. Overstated framework claims are a common greenwashing theory.",
 "Remove the SEC rules as a \"reference framework\" (or describe their status accurately and state that the report is not prepared to comply with them). Change \"referenced IFRS S2\" to \"informed by\" and add a statement that the report does not purport to comply fully with IFRS S2, or provide a content index showing which S2 requirements are addressed and which are not. Similarly limit claims that the inventory \"follows\" the GHG Protocol until the gaps in Issues 6, 12 and 19 are fixed.")

issue(12,"High","Scope 3 described as \"comprehensive\"; omissions and method misdescriptions",
